exercises.heading: Kwame's Reading Journey
exercises.subtitle: A heartwarming story about how asking for help and practicing every day can turn reading challenges into reading success

slides.title: Kwame's Reading Challenge
slides.text: Kwame loved stories, but reading was really hard for him. The words seemed to dance around on the page, and he felt frustrated when he couldn't keep up with his classmates.

slides.title: Asking for Help
slides.text: One day, Kwame decided to ask his big sister Akosua for help. "Can you teach me to read faster?" he asked hopefully. She smiled warmly and said, "Of course! I'd love to help you."

slides.title: Learning Together
slides.text: Akosua showed Kwame special tricks for reading. She taught him to follow along with his finger and to sound out difficult words. Reading together made it so much more fun!

slides.title: Practice Every Night
slides.text: Every evening after dinner, Kwame and Akosua would sit together and read. Some nights they read adventure stories, other nights they read about animals or faraway places.

slides.title: Success!
slides.text: After weeks of practice, Kwame discovered he could read much faster! He felt proud and confident. Now he could enjoy all the wonderful stories he had always wanted to read by himself.

modules.title: Habits Module
modules.description: Safe, Smart & Responsible Use of Technology. Digital responsibility means using devices in a safe and respectful way, making good choices online, protecting yourself and others, and managing screen time wisely.

techResponsiblyWelcome.intro: Every device has an owner — you. This week we power up our "responsible mode" and learn what it means to use phones, tablets and computers safely, kindly and in balance.
techResponsiblyWelcome.objectiveText: Learners understand how to use devices safely and responsibly.
techResponsiblyWelcome.pillarsHeading: Responsible use rests on three things…

pillars.title: Stay safe
pillars.text: Guard your name, photos and passwords.

pillars.title: Be respectful
pillars.text: Treat people online the way you would face to face.

pillars.title: Keep balance
pillars.text: Know when to put the screen down.

techResponsiblyWelcome.footerNote: A short, friendly lesson for our beginner class.

Responsible users think before they act.

exercises.heading: The Shared Tablet

slides.title: A Shared Tablet
slides.text: Yaw and his sister shared a tablet at home. One day, while using it, Yaw saw a message pop up.

slides.title: A Tempting Message
slides.text: “Click here to win a prize!” the message said. Yaw was excited. He almost clicked it.

slides.title: He Remembers
slides.text: Then he remembered what his teacher said: “Not everything online is safe.”

slides.title: He Asks First
slides.text: Instead of clicking, he called his older sister to check the message.

slides.title: The Right Thing
slides.text: She checked it and said, “This could be dangerous. You did the right thing.”

slides.title: Careful and Proud
slides.text: Later, their mother praised Yaw for being careful. Yaw realised that being responsible online means thinking before acting.

exercises.heading: Think & Apply
exercises.subtitle: Pick the answer that fits best — if it's not quite right, you'll get to try again!

questions.feedbackText: Yes — his older sister checked the message with him.

privacyVaultWelcome.intro: Some things about you are private — like treasure kept in a vault. This week we learn what personal information is and how to keep it locked away safely online.
privacyVaultWelcome.objectiveText: Learners understand how to protect personal information online.
privacyVaultWelcome.footerNote: A short, friendly lesson for our beginner class.

exercises.subtitle: Follow along as Kojo learns that not everyone online is safe — and privacy matters.

slides.text: He ignored the message and told his older brother what had happened.

slides.title: A Smart Decision
slides.text: His brother said, “That was a smart decision.”

slides.title: Privacy Matters
slides.text: Kojo learned that not everyone online is safe — and privacy matters.

screenBalanceWelcome.intro: Screens are fun — but a good day has room for many things. This week we look at how screen time fits around school, play, family and sleep, and we practise the self-control it takes to stop when it is time to stop.
screenBalanceWelcome.clockCaption: Screens get a slice — not the whole day.
screenBalanceWelcome.objectiveText: Learners manage screen time and practise self-control.
screenBalanceWelcome.strategiesHeading: Ways to stay in control of screen time…

strategies.title: Set a timer
strategies.text: Decide how long before you start — and stop when it rings.

strategies.title: Pause and breathe
strategies.text: When you feel "just one more", take a breath and choose.

strategies.title: Swap for something
strategies.text: Trade a scroll for a walk, a game outside or a chat.

strategies.title: Screens off early
strategies.text: Put devices away well before bedtime so sleep comes easily.

screenBalanceWelcome.footerNote: A short, friendly lesson for our beginner class.

exercises.title: Screen-Health Scan

statements.text: Screen time does not affect your sleep.

statements.text: Balance is important with screen time.

slides.title: A Hard Start

slides.title: Feeling Better

slides.title: Discipline Matters

practices.title: Pause first

practices.title: No mean jokes
practices.text: Teasing and name-calling still hurt through a screen.

imaginationSparkWelcome.objectiveText: Learners understand that creativity means thinking in new and different ways.

ways.title: New ideas

slides.text: Efua loved drawing but sometimes felt shy to show her work.

slides.title: The Art Display
slides.text: One day, her teacher announced an art display.

slides.title: A Simple Plan
slides.text: Efua decided to try. She followed a simple plan.

slides.title: Step 1 — Imagine
slides.text: She imagined a beautiful village.

slides.title: Step 2 — Draw
slides.text: She drew houses, trees, and people.

slides.title: Step 3 — Colour
slides.text: She carefully coloured everything.

slides.title: Step 4 — Details
slides.text: She added small details like birds and flowers. When she finished, she felt proud.

slides.title: Creativity Grows
slides.text: At the display, her classmates admired her work. One said, “I love your drawing!” Efua smiled. She learned that creativity grows when you express it.

modules.title: Strategizing Module
modules.description: Theme: Developing Cognitive Skills. Duration: 4 Weeks. What is Strategizing? Strategizing means thinking ahead and making a plan to solve a problem or reach a goal.

strategyBlueprintWelcome.intro: A strategy is a plan that helps solve a problem. Before we rush in, we look at the whole picture, think a few moves ahead, and draw a route to where we want to be.
strategyBlueprintWelcome.calloutText: A strategy is the dotted line — the thought-out path that goes around what is in the way.
strategyBlueprintWelcome.objectiveText: Learners understand that a strategy is a plan that helps solve problems.

traits.title: Has a goal
traits.text: You know exactly what you are trying to reach.

traits.title: Thinks ahead
traits.text: You picture the next few steps before you take them.

traits.title: Has a plan
traits.text: You choose the steps that get you there.

strategyBlueprintWelcome.footerNote: A short, friendly lesson for our beginner class.

exercises.title: Smart Choices
exercises.intro: Each goal has one smart plan — the choice that thinks ahead. Lock in every smart move to fill the plan track.

questions.goal: You want to build the tallest block tower.
questions.smartWhy: A strong, wide base first means the tower can go higher without falling.

questions.goal: You want to finish your homework quickly.

questions.smartWhy: Taking it one question at a time keeps you focused so you get it done and get it right.

questions.smartWhy: Thinking about your next move is planning ahead — that is what a strategy is.

questions.goal: You want to clean your room.

Looking for matching shapes is a plan — it gives you a way in when the first try does not work.

exercises.parentNote: Parents, please assist your ward with this exercise.

exercises.heading: Kofi's Football Plan
exercises.subtitle: Follow along as Kofi turns a losing game around by thinking ahead.

slides.title: Football After School
slides.text: Kofi loved playing football with his friends after school.

slides.title: The Team Keeps Losing
slides.text: One afternoon, their team kept losing the game. Every player ran after the ball at the same time. No one stayed near the goal, and no one passed the ball.

slides.title: Kofi Spots the Problem
slides.text: Kofi watched carefully and noticed the problem.

slides.title: "Let’s Try Something Different"
slides.text: During a break, he said, “Let’s try something different.” He suggested a strategy: one player guards the goal, two players pass the ball, and one player stays ready to shoot.

slides.title: The Plan in Action
slides.text: When the game started again, the team followed Kofi's plan. The ball moved quickly between players.

slides.title: Ama Scores!
slides.text: Soon, Ama scored a goal. Everyone cheered.

slides.title: Thinking Ahead Changes the Game
slides.text: Kofi realized that thinking ahead can change the game.

exercises.heading: Discussion Points
exercises.subtitle: Pick the best answer for each one — if it's not quite right, you'll get to try again!

questions.feedbackText: Right — every player ran after the ball at once, so no one guarded the goal or passed.
Yes — he gave each player a job so the team worked as a plan.
Exactly — following the plan moved the ball quickly and Ama scored.
Right — he watched, spotted the problem, and thought ahead.
Yes — a plan helps with games, homework, chores and lots more.

exercises.title: My First Strategy
exercises.intro: Pick one everyday task and turn it into a plan. Think ahead, then write three clear steps that get the job done.

exercises.subtitle: A strategy helps me stop, think ahead, and choose my steps. When I know my plan, hard things feel smaller.
exercises.trainerQuote: A good plan turns a big problem into small, doable steps — that is what a strategy does.
exercises.keyTakeawayQuote: Thinking ahead can change the game.
exercises.footerTagline: Stop. Think ahead. Make a plan. 🧭

pauseButtonWelcome.intro: The best move is not always the first move. This week we practise the pause — that small stop between what happens and what we do, where a better choice is made.
pauseButtonWelcome.objectiveText: Learners understand that pausing to think helps us choose better actions.

ways.title: Take a breath
ways.text: Slow down so your first feeling does not decide for you.

ways.title: Picture what happens next
ways.text: Think a step ahead: what will this choice lead to?

ways.title: Pick the better action
ways.text: Choose the move that helps, not the fastest one.

pauseButtonWelcome.footerNote: A short, friendly lesson for our beginner class.

statements.text: Thinking before acting can prevent mistakes.
statements.because: A short pause gives you time to spot a problem before it happens.
A strategy is a plan — planning always takes some thinking first.

statements.text: Planning can help finish work faster.
statements.because: When you know your steps, you waste less time wondering what to do next.

statements.text: It is always best to act immediately.
statements.because: Sometimes a quick pause to think leads to a much better choice.

statements.text: Thinking about choices helps you decide.
statements.because: Looking at your options is how you pick the one that works best.

exercises.heading: Ama and the School Fair
exercises.subtitle: Follow along as Ama helps her class stop, think, and get organized.

slides.title: Getting Ready for the Fair
slides.text: Ama's class was preparing bracelets for the school fair.

slides.title: Everyone Works Randomly
slides.text: At first, everyone worked randomly. Some students searched for beads. Others cut strings. A few tried making bracelets.

slides.title: A Messy Table
slides.text: Soon the table was messy. Beads rolled everywhere.

slides.title: "Let’s Think First"
slides.text: Ama paused and said, "Let’s think first."

slides.title: Ama's Plan
slides.text: She suggested a plan: one person sorts beads, one person cuts strings, and two people make bracelets. The group agreed.

slides.title: The Work Gets Organized
slides.text: Soon the work became organized. By the end of the day, they had many beautiful bracelets ready to sell.

slides.title: Thinking First Saves Time
slides.text: Ama learned that thinking first saves time and effort.

exercises.heading: Discussion Points
exercises.subtitle: Pick True or False for each one — if it's not quite right, you'll get to try again!

questions.prompt: Ama noticed the group was confused.
questions.feedbackText: Right — she saw the messy table and beads rolling everywhere.
Yes — she gave everyone a job: sort beads, cut strings, make bracelets.

questions.prompt: The group worked faster after planning.
questions.feedbackText: Right — the work became organized and they finished many bracelets.

questions.prompt: The group finished because they were lucky.
questions.feedbackText: It was not luck — the plan is what made the work go well.

questions.prompt: Thinking before acting can help groups work better.
questions.feedbackText: Yes — a short pause to plan helps everyone know what to do.

exercises.title: Pause and Plan

exercises.sayItText: I stop, I think, and I choose the best plan.

exercises.heading: Yaw and the Lost Keys
exercises.subtitle: Follow along as Yaw stays calm and searches step by step.

slides.title: A Simple Errand
slides.text: Yaw's mother asked him to bring the house keys from the living room table.

slides.title: The Keys Are Missing
slides.text: But when Yaw looked, the keys were missing. At first, he felt worried.

slides.title: Stop and Think
slides.text: Then he stopped and thought. Instead of shouting or blaming someone, he made a strategy.

slides.title: Search Step by Step
slides.text: He searched step by step. First, he checked the sofa.

slides.title: One Place at a Time
slides.text: Then the kitchen table. Then near the door.

slides.title: Found Them!
slides.text: Finally, he looked behind the shoe rack. There were the keys.

slides.title: A Step-by-Step Lesson
slides.text: Yaw smiled and said, "Searching step by step helps you find things faster."

exercises.sayItText: If my first plan does not work, I try a different one.

goalPathWelcome.objectiveText: Learners understand that strategies help us reach goals step by step.

exercises.heading: Esi's Reading Goal
exercises.subtitle: Follow along as Esi turns a hard goal into a simple 3-step plan.

slides.title: A Reading Goal
slides.text: Esi wanted to become a better reader.

slides.title: The Hard Part
slides.text: Some of her classmates could read long stories easily, but she struggled with difficult words.

slides.title: She Makes a Strategy
slides.text: Instead of giving up, Esi made a strategy. Her plan was simple.

slides.title: Her 3-Step Plan
slides.text: 1. Read for ten minutes every day. 2. Write down new words. 3. Ask questions about difficult parts.

slides.title: Slow at First
slides.text: At first reading felt slow.

slides.title: Something Changed
slides.text: But after several weeks something changed. She could read longer stories without stopping.

slides.title: A Whole Chapter Book
slides.text: One afternoon she finished an entire chapter book. Esi felt proud.

slides.title: Small Strategies, Big Success
slides.text: She realized that small strategies lead to big success.

exercises.heading: Discussion Points

modules.title: Thinking Module
modules.description: Theme: Developing Cognitive Skills.

attentionLensWelcome.intro: Paying attention means putting your mind on one thing and really noticing it. When we look closely, small details come into focus and the things trying to pull us away fade out.
attentionLensWelcome.calloutText: The lens is your attention — whatever you point it at gets clear, and everything else goes blurry.
attentionLensWelcome.objectiveText: Learners will strengthen focus and observation skills by identifying details and avoiding distractions.

traits.title: Notices details
traits.text: You spot the little things other people walk past.

traits.title: Blocks distractions
traits.text: You let the noise go by without following it.

traits.title: Stays with it
traits.text: You keep your mind on one thing until it is done.

attentionLensWelcome.footerNote: A short, friendly lesson for our beginner class.

exercises.intro: Look carefully at Picture A and Picture B. They are almost the same — but a few things have changed. Study both pictures, then answer every question in your own words.

exercises.heading: Kojo and the Missing Instructions
exercises.subtitle: A mini story about slowing down and looking carefully.

slides.title: Kojo Loves Building
slides.text: Kojo loved building blocks. His favourite thing was snapping the little pieces together to make something new.

slides.title: In a Hurry
slides.text: One day, he rushed to build a toy car without reading the instructions. He wanted it finished right away.

slides.title: Pushing Pieces Together
slides.text: He pushed the pieces together quickly, not really looking at where each one was supposed to go.

slides.title: The Wheels Fall Off
slides.text: But the wheels kept falling off. Every time Kojo moved the car, another wheel dropped to the floor.

slides.title: Ama Asks a Question
slides.text: His sister Ama said, "Did you look carefully at the steps?" Kojo shook his head. He had not looked at them at all.

slides.title: Slowing Down
slides.text: This time, he slowed down. He looked at each picture. He counted the pieces. He matched the colours carefully.

slides.title: It Rolls Perfectly
slides.text: When he finished, the car rolled perfectly across the floor. Nothing wobbled and nothing fell off.

slides.title: What Kojo Learned
slides.text: Kojo smiled. "I just needed to think and look carefully."

exercises.takeHome: Good thinking begins with careful attention.

solutionPathWelcome.intro: A problem is just something in your way. We can get past it with three calm steps: work out what the problem really is, think of a few ways to fix it, then choose the best one.
solutionPathWelcome.calloutText: The path is the plan — one clear problem, a few ideas, and the best choice at the end.
solutionPathWelcome.objectiveText: Learners will practise simple problem-solving steps: identify the problem, think of solutions, choose the best one.

traits.title: Names the problem
traits.text: You say exactly what is wrong before trying to fix it.

traits.title: Thinks of options
traits.text: You come up with more than one way to solve it.

traits.title: Weighs the choices
traits.text: You pick the idea that works best, not just the first one.

solutionPathWelcome.footerNote: A short, friendly lesson for our beginner class.

exercises.heading: Esi and the Puzzle
exercises.subtitle: A mini story about solving a problem step by step.

slides.title: A New Puzzle
slides.text: Esi received a 50-piece puzzle. She tipped all the pieces onto the table, excited to see the picture come together.

slides.title: Forcing the Pieces
slides.text: She tried forcing pieces together when they did not fit. The picture looked wrong, and nothing lined up.

slides.title: Dad Asks a Question
slides.text: Her father saw her frowning and asked, "What's the problem?"

slides.title: Naming the Problem
slides.text: Esi paused and thought about it. "The pieces don't match," she said.

slides.title: Edges First
slides.text: She made a plan. First, she sorted out all the edge pieces and built the frame.

slides.title: Grouping Colours
slides.text: Then she grouped the pieces by colour. Slowly, the picture began to form.

slides.title: Step by Step Works
slides.text: Instead of rushing, she had used a plan. When she finished, she said, "Thinking step by step works!"

exercises.takeHome: Problems shrink when we think step by step.

memoryWorkshopWelcome.intro: Recall means bringing something back to mind when you need it. Our memory works better with a little help — like putting things into groups, and saying them over again until they stick.
memoryWorkshopWelcome.groupingCaption: Sorting a long list into small groups makes it much easier to remember.
memoryWorkshopWelcome.repetitionCaption: Saying something over and over helps your memory hold on to it.
memoryWorkshopWelcome.calloutText: Grouping and repetition are two simple tricks that make your memory stronger.
memoryWorkshopWelcome.objectiveText: Learners will strengthen memory by practising recall strategies such as grouping and repetition.

traits.title: Sorts things
traits.text: You put what you learn into groups that go together.

traits.title: Practises
traits.text: You say or do it again and again until it sticks.

traits.title: Recalls it
traits.text: You can bring the information back when you need it.

memoryWorkshopWelcome.footerNote: A short, friendly lesson for our beginner class.

exercises.heading: Yaw and the Spelling Words
exercises.subtitle: A mini story about training your memory with practice.

slides.title: Forgetting the Words
slides.text: Yaw kept forgetting his spelling words. No matter how he tried, they would not stay in his head.

slides.title: Feeling Frustrated
slides.text: He felt frustrated. It seemed like the words just slipped away every time.

slides.title: The Teacher’s Trick
slides.text: His teacher showed him a trick: group similar words together so they are easier to hold in mind.

slides.title: Say Them Aloud
slides.text: Next, she told him to repeat the words aloud, over and over, until they felt familiar.

slides.title: Use Them in Sentences
slides.text: Then he used each word in a sentence of his own, so it had a meaning he could remember.

slides.title: A Little Every Day
slides.text: Instead of cramming the night before, Yaw practised a little every day.

slides.title: Test Day
slides.text: On test day, he remembered almost all of them. Yaw realised memory grows with practice.

exercises.takeHome: Your brain gets stronger when you train it.

smartChoiceForecastWelcome.intro: A smart choice is one you think through first. Before you decide, you picture what will happen next — the consequence — and then pick the path that leads somewhere good.
smartChoiceForecastWelcome.calloutText: The same moment, two choices — thinking ahead is what changes where you end up.
smartChoiceForecastWelcome.objectiveText: Learners will use logical thinking to predict consequences before making decisions.

traits.title: Pauses first
traits.text: You stop for a moment before you decide.

traits.title: Looks ahead
traits.text: You picture what will happen after each choice.

traits.title: Picks wisely
traits.text: You choose the path that leads to a good result.

smartChoiceForecastWelcome.footerNote: A short, friendly lesson for our beginner class.

exercises.heading: Adwoa's Choice
exercises.subtitle: A mini story about thinking ahead before you decide.

slides.title: Two Things at Once
slides.text: Adwoa had homework to do and her favourite TV show was starting at the same time.

slides.title: Thinking It Through
slides.text: She stopped to think. "If I watch TV first, I may be too tired to do my homework later."

slides.title: Homework First
slides.text: So she decided to finish her homework first, while her mind was fresh.

slides.title: No Stress
slides.text: Later, she enjoyed her show with nothing left to worry about. Adwoa learned that thinking ahead makes life easier.

exercises.takeHome: Smart thinkers think ahead.

exercises.heading: Ama's Weekly Budget
exercises.subtitle: See how a simple weekly plan changed things for Ama.

slides.title: Ama's Weekly Money
slides.text: Ama received a little money every week.

slides.title: A Simple Plan
slides.text: Before she spent any of it, Ama made a simple plan for where her money would go.

slides.title: Part 1: School Needs
slides.text: First, she set aside money for the things she needed for school.

slides.title: Part 2: Savings
slides.text: Next, she put some money into her savings — every single week.

slides.title: Part 3: A Small Treat
slides.text: Last, she kept a little for one small treat she could enjoy.

slides.title: Hard at First
slides.text: Sticking to the plan was difficult at first — it was tempting to spend it all at once.

slides.title: It Got Easier
slides.text: Over time, Ama stopped running out of money, and she started saving more and more.

slides.title: Planning Gives Control
slides.text: Her friends often had nothing left by the weekend — but Ama always did. She realised that planning your money gives you control.

exercises.takeHome: Planning gives you control of your money.

exercises.heading: Think & Apply
exercises.subtitle: Pick the result each money habit leads to — a wrong pick lets you try again.

questions.feedbackText: Right — a budget puts you in control of your money.

questions.prompt: What does planning ahead lead to?
questions.feedbackText: That is it — planning ahead makes your choices clear.

exercises.parentNote: Parents/guardians: please help your ward set up their jar or box and check in each day. The savings can be real or pretend.
exercises.allDoneText: You saved something for 5 days and tracked it. That is how a saving habit begins!

exercises.statement: I can save money for something important.
exercises.reinforceLine: Every coin you save brings you closer to something that matters to you.

savingStepsWelcome.subtitle: Saving is something you practise, one small step at a time. Let's find ways to do it!
savingStepsWelcome.objectiveText: Learners identify ways to practise saving.

exercises.heading: Match the Money Words
exercises.subtitle: Tap a word, then tap the meaning that fits it.
exercises.pickWordHint: Tap a word on the left to begin.
exercises.pickMeaningHint: Now tap the meaning that fits.
exercises.allDoneText: You know what these money words mean. Ready for the next part?
exercises.parentNote: Parents/guardians: please sit with your ward for this exercise and talk each match through together.

exercises.heading: What We Learned
exercises.subtitle: Three things to remember about saving.

exercises.prompt: Challenge of the Week: Save or Spend?
exercises.title: Save or Spend?
exercises.intro: Each day, when you get money, decide what to do with it — and say why.
exercises.parentNote: Parents/guardians: please check in with your ward each day and talk about what they chose and why.
exercises.allDoneText: You made a choice every day and explained it. That is how smart savers think!

exercises.statement: I can choose to save instead of spend.
exercises.reinforceLine: Every time you pause and choose to save, you are building a habit that lasts.

modules.title: Discipline Module
modules.description: Theme: Developing Personal Responsibility & Self-Control. Discipline means doing the right thing even when it is hard, controlling your actions and choices, and following rules and routines.

disciplineCompassWelcome.objectiveText: Learners understand discipline as making good choices consistently.
disciplineCompassWelcome.footerNote: A short, friendly lesson for our beginner class.

exercises.heading: What is Discipline?
exercises.subtitle: Answer each question to earn a shield. Light them all to move on!

questions.feedbackText: Yes! Discipline is making good choices.
Right — a disciplined person does the right thing.

questions.prompt: If your teacher is not watching, you should:
questions.feedbackText: Exactly — you behave well even when no one is watching.
That is it — discipline helps you succeed.
Well done — following rules shows discipline.

exercises.allDoneText: You know that discipline is making good choices — again and again.
exercises.parentNote: Grown-ups: talk with your child about a time they made a good choice on their own.

exercises.heading: Kofi's Choice
exercises.subtitle: A short story about choosing what is right, not just what is fun.

slides.title: Kofi Loves Football
slides.text: Kofi loved playing football. One afternoon, he had homework to complete before playing.

slides.title: His Friends Call
slides.text: His friends called him outside. "Come and play!" they shouted. Kofi felt excited, but he remembered his teacher's instructions.

slides.title: Homework First
slides.text: He sat down and completed his homework first. It wasn't easy — he wanted to run outside. But he stayed focused.

slides.title: Then He Plays
slides.text: After finishing, he went to play.

slides.title: A Proud Day
slides.text: The next day, his teacher praised him for his work. Kofi felt proud.

exercises.takeHome: Discipline means choosing what is right, not just what is fun.

exercises.heading: Think & Try
exercises.subtitle: Pick the answer that fits best — if it's not quite right, you'll get to try again!

questions.prompt: What would happen if he played first?

exercises.heading: My Good Choices
exercises.description: Each day this week, write or say one good choice you made — and one thing you did even when it was hard.
tags: One thing I did even when it was hard
exercises.confidenceQuote: I can make the right choice.
exercises.parentNote: Parents: please help your child keep their daily list this week.

exercises.prompt: I Can Make the Right Choice
exercises.subtitle: Discipline helps you make good choices — again and again, even when it is hard.
exercises.trainerQuote: Discipline helps you say: "I can make the right choice."
exercises.keyTakeawayQuote: I can make the right choice.
exercises.footerTagline: Discipline is making good choices. It is not always easy — and it leads to success.

selfControlDialWelcome.objectiveText: Learners understand discipline as controlling actions and emotions.
selfControlDialWelcome.footerNote: A short, friendly lesson for our beginner class.

exercises.heading: True or False?
exercises.subtitle: Judge each statement. Fill every breath dot to move on!

statements.feedbackText: Yes — self-control is controlling what you do.

statements.text: It is okay to shout when angry.
statements.feedbackText: Right — when angry, we pause instead of shouting.
Exactly — a pause gives you time to choose.
Correct — discipline means thinking first, not rushing.

statements.text: Taking deep breaths can help control emotions.
statements.feedbackText: Yes — slow breaths help calm big feelings.

exercises.allDoneText: You know self-control is pausing and choosing how to act.
exercises.parentNote: Grown-ups: practise one slow breath together when a big feeling shows up.

exercises.heading: Ama's Angry Moment
exercises.subtitle: A short story about pausing, breathing, and choosing how to react.

slides.title: Ama Loses the Game
slides.text: Ama was playing a game with her friend. Suddenly, she lost. Her friend laughed.

slides.title: Ama Feels Angry
slides.text: Ama felt angry. She wanted to shout and push her friend. But she stopped.

slides.title: She Remembers
slides.text: She remembered what her teacher said: "Take a deep breath."

slides.title: Ama Pauses
slides.text: Ama paused. She took a breath. Then she said, "I feel upset, but I will try again."

slides.title: Playing Peacefully
slides.text: Her friend smiled. They continued playing peacefully.

exercises.takeHome: Discipline means controlling your reactions, not just your actions.

exercises.heading: Think & Try
exercises.subtitle: Think back to the story. Pick True or False — a wrong pick lets you try again.

exercises.heading: Pause & Choose
exercises.description: When you feel angry, excited, or upset: Stop, take a deep breath, then choose your action. Afterwards, think: What did I feel? What did I choose?
exercises.confidenceQuote: I can control myself.
exercises.parentNote: Parents: help your child practise the Stop – Breathe – Choose steps when a big feeling comes up.

exercises.subtitle: Self-control means pausing, breathing, and choosing how to act — even when feelings are big.
exercises.trainerQuote: Self-control helps you say: "I can control myself."
exercises.footerTagline: Discipline includes self-control. You can pause before acting, and emotions can be managed.

routineLoopWelcome.objectiveText: Learners understand discipline as building good habits and routines.
routineLoopWelcome.footerNote: A short, friendly lesson for our beginner class.

exercises.heading: Match the Routine
exercises.subtitle: Drag each result onto the routine that leads to it. Match them all to move on!
exercises.allDoneText: Good routines lead to good results — every day.
exercises.parentNote: Grown-ups: name one routine you keep and the result it gives you.

exercises.heading: Yaw's New Routine
exercises.subtitle: A short story about how a daily routine builds discipline over time.

slides.title: Yaw Keeps Forgetting
slides.text: Yaw used to forget his books often. He rushed every morning. Sometimes he missed homework.

slides.title: A New Routine
slides.text: One day, his mother helped him create a routine: pack bag at night, sleep early, and wake up on time.

slides.title: It Felt Strange
slides.text: Yaw followed the routine. At first, it felt strange.

slides.title: It Got Easier
slides.text: But after a few days, it became easier. He stopped forgetting things.

slides.title: Teacher Notices
slides.text: His teacher noticed improvement.

exercises.takeHome: Discipline is built through daily habits.

exercises.heading: Think & Try
exercises.subtitle: Match each habit to the benefit it brings — a wrong pick lets you try again.

questions.prompt: What benefit comes from planning ahead?
What benefit comes from doing work early?
What benefit comes from staying organized?
What benefit comes from following a routine?
What benefit comes from practicing daily?

exercises.heading: My Daily Routine
exercises.description: Create your own routine — one thing for the Morning, one for After school, and one for Night — then follow it for 3 to 5 days.
exercises.confidenceQuote: I am organized and ready.
exercises.parentNote: Parents: help your child write their routine and check in each day for 3–5 days.

exercises.subtitle: A routine you follow every day builds discipline and makes life feel easier.
exercises.trainerQuote: Routines help you say: "I am organized and ready."
exercises.footerTagline: Discipline builds habits, routines make life easier, and practice leads to improvement.

consistencyStreakWelcome.objectiveText: Learners understand discipline as doing the right thing consistently.
consistencyStreakWelcome.footerNote: A short, friendly lesson for our beginner class.

exercises.heading: Put It in Order
exercises.subtitle: Tap the steps into the right order. Solve every one to move on!

questions.feedbackText: You plan first, then start, then finish.
First you know your duty, then act, then complete it.
Start it, repeat it, and it improves.
Understand it, do it, then submit it.
Think first, then act, then reflect on it.

exercises.allDoneText: Doing the right things in the right order builds discipline.
exercises.parentNote: Grown-ups: pick one everyday task and name its steps in order together.

exercises.heading: Efua Keeps Going
exercises.subtitle: A short story about staying consistent even when it feels hard.

slides.title: Efua Starts Studying
slides.text: Efua started studying every evening. At first, she was excited.

slides.title: She Feels Tired
slides.text: After a few days, she felt tired. She wanted to stop.

slides.title: I Must Be Consistent
slides.text: But she reminded herself: "I must be consistent." She continued, even on days she didn't feel like it.

slides.title: Results Improve
slides.text: After some weeks, her results improved. Her confidence grew.

slides.title: What Efua Learned
slides.text: Efua learned that discipline is not just starting — it is continuing even when it is hard.

exercises.takeHome: Discipline is not just starting. It is continuing even when it is hard.

exercises.heading: Think & Try
exercises.subtitle: Put Efua's journey in order — pick the step for each place. A wrong pick lets you try again.

exercises.heading: My Discipline Tracker
exercises.description: For 5 days, track one task you completed, one moment you used self-control, and one routine you followed. Then reflect: What did I do well? What was difficult? What will I improve?
exercises.confidenceQuote: I keep going even when it is hard.
exercises.parentNote: Parents: help your child keep the tracker for 5 days and talk through the reflection questions together.

exercises.subtitle: Consistency means continuing — doing the right thing again and again, even on hard days.
exercises.trainerQuote: Consistency helps you say: "I keep going even when it is hard."
exercises.keyTakeawayQuote: I keep going even when it is hard.
exercises.footerTagline: You can now make good choices, control your actions and emotions, build routines, and stay consistent.

modules.title: Service Module
modules.description: Theme: Helping Others & Making a Difference. Service means noticing when someone needs help, choosing to lend a hand, and doing small kind acts that make life better for the people and places around us.

serviceHandsWelcome.handsMark: A little help goes a long way
serviceHandsWelcome.objectiveText: Learners will understand the meaning of service and identify simple ways to help others.
serviceHandsWelcome.footerNote: A short, friendly lesson for our beginner class.

exercises.heading: What is Service?
exercises.subtitle: Answer each question to drop a heart in the jar. Fill it up to move on!

questions.feedbackText: Yes! Service is helping others without expecting a reward.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of service?
questions.feedbackText: Right — helping a friend clean up is service.
Exactly — people serve to make a difference.
That is it — service helps people feel happy and supported.
Well done — service can happen anywhere.

exercises.allDoneText: You know that service is helping others — anywhere, without expecting a reward.
exercises.parentNote: Grown-ups: talk with your child about a small way they helped someone this week.

exercises.prompt: Story: Ama and the Heavy Bucket
exercises.heading: Ama and the Heavy Bucket
exercises.subtitle: Follow along as Ama chooses to help on her way home from school.

slides.title: On the Way Home
slides.text: Ama was walking home from school when she saw an elderly woman struggling to carry a heavy bucket of water.

slides.title: A Quiet Thought
slides.text: Ama was tired and wanted to go home quickly. She paused and thought, “Someone should help her.” Then she realised — she could help.

slides.title: “May I Help You?”
slides.text: She walked up and said, “Please, may I help you?” The woman smiled warmly and handed her the bucket.

slides.title: Walking Together
slides.text: As they walked together, the woman said, “You have a kind heart.” Ama reached home later than usual — but she felt proud and happy.

slides.title: That Is Service
slides.text: That night, she told her mother what she did. Her mother smiled and said, “That is what service looks like — helping when you can.”

exercises.heading: Discussion Points
exercises.subtitle: Pick the answer that fits best — if it's not quite right, you'll get to try again!

questions.feedbackText: Yes — she saw an elderly woman struggling with a heavy bucket.
Right — she was tired and wanted to get home quickly.
Exactly — she offered to help and carried the bucket.
That is it — she was happy and grateful, and said Ama has a kind heart.
Well done — small acts of service matter.

exercises.title: One Act of Service
exercises.intro: This week, do one helpful act each day. Then log it here.
exercises.didPlaceholder: e.g. I helped wash the dishes
exercises.reactionPlaceholder: e.g. She smiled and said thank you
exercises.parentNote: Grown-ups: help your child notice a small way to serve each day, and talk about how it felt.
exercises.allDoneText: You helped someone every day this week — that is what service looks like.

exercises.statement: I can help others in simple ways every day.
exercises.reinforceLine: Service is not about big things — it is helping when you can, wherever you are.

serviceSpotsWelcome.objectiveText: Learners will identify ways to serve in their immediate environment.
serviceSpotsWelcome.footerNote: A short, friendly lesson for our beginner class.

exercises.heading: Where Does It Belong?
exercises.subtitle: Drag each helpful act into the place it happens. Sort them all to move on!
exercises.allDoneText: You can serve at home and at school — helpful acts belong everywhere.
exercises.parentNote: Grown-ups: talk with your child about one way they help at home and one way they help at school.

exercises.heading: Kojo's Change
exercises.subtitle: Follow along as Kojo learns that serving others helps him grow too.

slides.title: Kojo Avoids Helping
slides.text: Kojo always left his chores for others. At school, he also avoided helping.

slides.title: Group Work
slides.text: One day, his teacher assigned group work. Kojo refused to help. His group struggled and did poorly.

slides.title: The Teacher’s Words
slides.text: Later, the teacher said, “Service is not just helping others — it helps you grow too.”

slides.title: Kojo Decides to Change
slides.text: The next week, Kojo decided to change: he helped clean the classroom, he supported his group, and he helped at home.

slides.title: A Better Person
slides.text: Slowly, people began to trust him more. Kojo realised that serving others made him a better person.

exercises.heading: Discussion Points
exercises.subtitle: Choose the place each helpful act belongs — if it's not quite right, you'll get to try again!

questions.feedbackText: Yes — washing dishes is a way to serve at home.
Right — helping a classmate with homework is serving at school.
Exactly — cleaning the classroom is serving at school.
Well done — helping your parents is serving at home.

exercises.title: Service Tracker – My Environment
exercises.intro: For 5 days, do at least 2 acts of service each day — at home or at school. Log each one here.
exercises.resultPlaceholder: e.g. The kitchen was clean and Mum was happy
exercises.summaryHeading: At the end of the week
exercises.mostHelpfulPlaceholder: Which act do you think helped the most, and why?
exercises.parentNote: Grown-ups: help your child spot 2 ways to serve each day and talk about the results together.
exercises.allDoneText: You served at home and at school every day this week.

exercises.statement: I can serve at home and at school.
exercises.reinforceLine: Wherever you are, there is a way to help — at home, at school, everywhere.

serviceKindnessWelcome.objectiveText: Learners will understand how kindness and responsibility relate to service.
serviceKindnessWelcome.footerNote: A short, friendly lesson for our beginner class.

exercises.heading: Kindness & Responsibility
exercises.subtitle: True or false? Judge each one right to light a star. Light them all to move on!

statements.feedbackText: Yes — service is done with a kind heart.
Right — you have to follow through on what you promised to do.
Correct — ignoring others is the opposite of service.
Exactly — helping is one way we show we care.
Well done — responsibility matters a lot in service.

exercises.allDoneText: Service takes kindness and responsibility working together.
exercises.parentNote: Grown-ups: talk with your child about a time being responsible helped them keep a promise to help.

exercises.heading: The Forgotten Lunch
exercises.subtitle: Follow along as Esi turns one small act of kindness into a big change for a classmate.

slides.title: Esi Notices Lina
slides.text: Esi noticed her classmate, Lina, sitting quietly during lunch. She realised Lina had no food.

slides.title: A Hard Choice
slides.text: At first, Esi hesitated — she was hungry too. Then she remembered what her teacher said about kindness and responsibility.

slides.title: Esi Shares Her Lunch
slides.text: She shared her lunch with Lina.

slides.title: Lina Grows
slides.text: The next day, Lina smiled more, participated in class, and became more confident.

slides.title: One Small Act
slides.text: Esi realised that one small act could change someone’s day.

exercises.heading: Discussion Points
exercises.subtitle: True or false? If it's not quite right, you'll get to try again!

questions.feedbackText: Right — Esi noticed Lina and shared her lunch.

questions.prompt: Sharing is a form of service.
questions.feedbackText: Yes — sharing what you have is one way to serve.
Exactly — one kind act helped Lina feel more confident.
Correct — service takes effort, like Esi giving up part of her lunch.
Well done — being responsible helps us follow through on kindness.

exercises.title: Kindness in Action Plan
exercises.intro: Choose 3 specific acts of kindness to do this week. Plan each one, then come back and note what changed after you do it.
exercises.actPlaceholder: e.g. Help my little sister with her reading
exercises.doneCheckLabel: I completed this act of kindness
exercises.changedPlaceholder: e.g. She read a whole page on her own and felt proud
exercises.parentNote: Grown-ups: help your child pick 3 realistic acts of kindness and talk about what changed afterwards.
exercises.allDoneText: Three planned acts of kindness, all done — that is service with kindness and responsibility.

exercises.statement: I show kindness and responsibility through service.
exercises.reinforceLine: When kindness meets responsibility, your service really makes a difference.

serviceRippleWelcome.objectiveText: Learners will recognise their ability to create positive change through service.
serviceRippleWelcome.footerNote: A short, friendly lesson for our beginner class.

exercises.title: Finish the Sentence
exercises.intro: Tap a word, then tap the blank it belongs in. Fill every blank to move on!

sentences.praise: Yes — service creates change.
Right — helping others makes a difference.
Exactly — you can help your community.
That is it — small actions can have a big impact.
Well done — service shows care.

exercises.allDoneText: Your service can create change and make a real difference.
exercises.parentNote: Grown-ups: talk with your child about one change they would like to make in their community.

exercises.heading: The Clean-Up Team
exercises.subtitle: Follow along as a group of children stop complaining and start making a difference.

slides.title: A Dirty Playground
slides.text: A group of children noticed their playground was always dirty. They complained — but nothing changed.

slides.title: Adjoa Has an Idea
slides.text: One day, Adjoa said, “Instead of complaining, let’s do something.”

slides.title: The Clean-Up Team
slides.text: They formed a small clean-up team: they picked litter, they encouraged others, and they made simple posters.

slides.title: Others Join In
slides.text: At first, people laughed. But slowly, others joined. Within weeks, the playground became clean — and stayed clean.

slides.title: Making a Difference
slides.text: The children realised they didn’t need to be adults to make a difference.

exercises.heading: Discussion Points
exercises.subtitle: Finish each sentence — if it's not quite right, you'll get to try again!

questions.prompt: The children solved the problem by ______.
questions.feedbackText: Yes — they solved it by taking action.
Right — service can start with small steps.
Exactly — a good example encouraged others to join.
That is it — the result was a clean environment.
Well done — anyone can make a difference.

exercises.title: My Service Project
exercises.intro: Choose ONE small project to complete this week. Plan it clearly, do it, then come back and record what changed.
exercises.whatPlaceholder: e.g. Tidy and sweep the reading corner in my classroom
exercises.whoPlaceholder: e.g. My class and my teacher
exercises.changedPlaceholder: e.g. The reading corner is tidy and easy to use
exercises.benefitedPlaceholder: e.g. Everyone who reads there, and my teacher
exercises.parentNote: Grown-ups: help your child choose one realistic project, carry it out, and talk about the difference it made.
exercises.allDoneText: You planned it, you did it, and you made a real difference — that is service.

exercises.statement: I can make a positive difference through service.
exercises.reinforceLine: You have learned that anyone — including you — can serve and make a difference.

modules.title: Teamwork Module
modules.description: Theme: Working Together. Teamwork means doing your part, listening to others, sharing the load, and helping the group reach a goal that no one could reach alone.

teamworkPuzzleWelcome.objectiveText: Learners will understand what teamwork means and identify basic teamwork behaviours.
teamworkPuzzleWelcome.footerNote: A short, friendly lesson for our beginner class.

exercises.heading: What is Teamwork?
exercises.subtitle: Answer each question to add a hand to the stack. Get everyone in to move on!

options.text: Working with others to achieve something

questions.feedbackText: Yes! Teamwork is working with others to achieve something.
Right — sharing ideas is teamwork.
Exactly — a good team member listens to others.

questions.prompt: When you are in a team, you should:
questions.feedbackText: That is it — in a team you help others.
Well done — teams make the work easier.

exercises.allDoneText: You know that teamwork means working together, listening, sharing, and helping.
exercises.parentNote: Grown-ups: talk with your child about a time they worked well with others.

exercises.heading: The Broken Bridge
exercises.subtitle: A story about four children who get more done once they stop arguing and each do what they are good at.

slides.title: Four Friends, One River
slides.text: In a small village, four children — Ama, Kojo, Esi, and Kofi — needed to cross a river to get to school. One day, the wooden bridge broke.

slides.title: Everyone Has an Idea
slides.text: Ama said, "Let's fix it together." Kojo replied, "I can carry wood." Esi said, "I will tie the ropes." Kofi added, "I'll make sure it is strong."

slides.title: The Arguing Starts
slides.text: At first, they argued about who should lead. Everyone wanted to be in charge. The work stopped.

slides.title: A Better Plan
slides.text: Then Ama said, "We won't finish if we keep arguing. Let's each do what we are good at." They agreed.

slides.title: Working Together
slides.text: Slowly, they worked together. By evening, the bridge was fixed.

slides.title: Across at Last
slides.text: The next day, they crossed safely — smiling and proud.

exercises.heading: Discussion Points
exercises.subtitle: Pick the answer that fits best — if it's not quite right, you'll get to try again!

questions.prompt: Why did the children fail at first?
questions.feedbackText: Yes — they argued about who should lead, and the work stopped.
Right — they listened to each other and each took a role.
Exactly — every child did their part.
That is it — teamwork helps solve problems.

questions.prompt: If they didn't work together, what would happen?
questions.feedbackText: Well done — without teamwork, they might never cross.

exercises.heading: Mini Team Mission
exercises.description: Ask a sibling or friend to do a small task together — clean a space, arrange books, or cook something simple. Divide the roles clearly before you start. Afterwards, think about how it went, then write or think about: "What made our teamwork good or difficult?"
exercises.confidenceQuote: I can work with others and share responsibilities.
exercises.parentNote: Parents: please help your child pick a task and notice how the roles were shared.

exercises.subtitle: Teamwork means doing your part and sharing the load, so the whole group can succeed.
exercises.trainerQuote: Teamwork helps you say: "I can work with others and share responsibilities."
exercises.keyTakeawayQuote: I can work with others and share responsibilities.
exercises.footerTagline: Teamwork means working together. Everyone has a role, and listening helps.

teamworkRolesWelcome.rolesMark: Everyone has a job to do
teamworkRolesWelcome.objectiveText: Learners will identify different roles in a team and understand responsibility.
teamworkRolesWelcome.footerNote: A short, friendly lesson for our beginner class.

exercises.heading: Match Role → Action
exercises.subtitle: Match each team role to what that person does. Match them all to move on!
exercises.allDoneText: You know what each team member does — and that every role matters.
exercises.parentNote: Grown-ups: talk with your child about which role they enjoy most in a team.

exercises.heading: The School Garden
exercises.subtitle: A story about a class that each takes a role to plant a garden — and keeps going when one job falls through.

slides.title: A Garden to Plant
slides.text: A class was asked to plant a garden.

slides.title: Everyone Takes a Role
slides.text: Yaw became the leader and organised the tasks. Adwoa watered the plants daily. Kwame brought the tools. Efua reminded everyone of the schedule.

slides.title: The Tools Are Missing
slides.text: One day, Kwame didn't bring the tools. Work stopped.

slides.title: The Team Works It Out
slides.text: Instead of blaming him, the team worked together. Adwoa shared her tools, and they continued.

slides.title: The Garden Grows
slides.text: After weeks, the garden grew beautifully.

exercises.heading: Discussion Points
exercises.subtitle: Match each situation to the role it needs. Tap a situation, then the role — if it is not quite right, you can try again.

exercises.heading: Role Explorer
exercises.description: Join or create a small group of 2–3 people. Assign roles — Leader, Helper, Speaker — and do one task together. Afterwards, reflect: which role did you play? Was it easy or hard? Would you like a different role next time?
exercises.confidenceQuote: I can take responsibility in a team.
exercises.parentNote: Parents: please help your child form a small group and pick a task to share.

exercises.subtitle: Every team needs each member to own their role — when you do your part, the whole team moves forward.
exercises.trainerQuote: Roles help you say: "I can take responsibility in a team."
exercises.keyTakeawayQuote: I can take responsibility in a team.
exercises.footerTagline: Everyone has a role. Roles make teamwork easier, and responsibility matters.

teamworkTalkWelcome.objectiveText: Learners will practise communication skills within teamwork.
teamworkTalkWelcome.footerNote: A short, friendly lesson for our beginner class.

exercises.heading: Talking in Teams
exercises.subtitle: Decide if each one is true or false. Fill the meter to move on!

statements.feedbackText: True — teams need to talk to work well together.
False — shouting makes teamwork harder.
True — listening is a big part of good teamwork.
False — ignoring others is the opposite of teamwork.
True — calm talking keeps a team working together.

slides.text: Kojo, Ama, Efua, and Selorm were paired together for the biggest group project of the term. Each of them saw the assignment a little differently.

slides.title: Kojo Takes the Lead
slides.text: Kojo is Choleric — confident and driven. He jumped straight in, organizing the team and setting deadlines so nothing would fall behind.

slides.title: Ama Sparks the Ideas
slides.text: Ama is Sanguine — fun and full of energy. She filled the group chat with creative ideas and kept everyone laughing, even during the stressful parts.

slides.title: Efua Perfects the Details
slides.text: Efua is Melancholic — thoughtful and precise. She double-checked every fact and made sure the project was accurate and well put together.

slides.title: Selorm Keeps the Peace
slides.text: Selorm is Phlegmatic — calm and easygoing. Whenever tempers rose, Selorm helped everyone slow down, listen, and find a middle ground.

slides.title: Stronger Together
slides.text: On presentation day, the project was a success — not despite their differences, but because of them. Each temperament brought something the others couldn't.

exercises.takeHome: Different temperaments can work together to achieve great results.

exercises.heading: The Late Project
exercises.subtitle: Step through Nana’s week — watch how the mood changes.

panels.caption: Nana had a big project due in two weeks. “Plenty of time,” she thought, and set it aside.
Days went by. She kept meaning to start, but there was always something else to do.
The night before, Nana stared at a blank page. Her heart raced and nothing came out.
Her friend Joel noticed. “Let’s not panic,” he said. “Let’s break it down together.”
They split the project into small daily steps, each with its own deadline on a checklist.
Nana worked one step at a time. Ticking each box felt good — progress beats panic.

exercises.takeaway: When a big task feels scary, breaking it into small daily steps turns panic into progress.

exercises.strategiesHeading: Five ways to choose your words well

strategies.title: Think Before Speaking
strategies.tip: Pause for a few seconds before talking to avoid saying something hurtful when angry.
strategies.example: Instead of blurting out "That's a dumb idea," try "I'm not sure that will work — what if we try it this way?"

strategies.title: Use Encouraging Phrases
strategies.tip: Use words that give hope or praise.
strategies.example: Replace "You're terrible at this game" with "You're improving every time — keep going!"

strategies.title: Be Clear and Kind in Feedback
strategies.tip: When giving feedback, include something positive first.
strategies.example: I like the colours you used in your poster. Maybe you could add a bigger title so it stands out even more.

strategies.title: Choose Words for the Situation
strategies.tip: If a friend is sad, speak softly and say something supportive.
strategies.example: I'm here for you. Want to talk about what happened?

strategies.title: Show Gratitude and Respect
strategies.tip: Simple words like "thank you," "please," and "I appreciate you" show confidence and respect.
strategies.example: Thanks for explaining that problem — it really helped me.

slides.text: "What if I forget my words? What if I lose?" Shane almost didn't sign up at all.

slides.title: Small Steps Forward
slides.text: Shane remembered what he'd learned all month — he practiced a little each day, spoke up in class, and tried things even when he wasn't sure.

slides.title: Goal Achieved!
slides.text: On debate day, Shane's voice shook a little — but he spoke anyway. He didn't win every round, but he walked off stage prouder than ever.

slides.title: What Shane Learned
